'MOLECULAR CHARACTERIZATION OF MALARIA VECTORS IN AGRICULTURAL AND RESIDENTIAL LAND USE TYPES IN WESTERN NORTH REGION: IMPLICATIONS FOR TARGETED CONTROL STRATEGIES
PROPOSAL SUMMARY
Malaria remains a significant public health challenge in Ghana. The disease is disproportionately distributed across the country with Western North Region Western North Region contributing significant prevalence of malaria cases. Land use changes are known to alter vector ecology. However, the molecular characterization of Anopheles populations in this transitional ecological zone where forest-savanna mosaics intersect with intensive agriculture remains understudied in this region. This study will integrate entomological inoculation rate (EIR), species-specific PCR, and Plasmodium detection (18S rRNA). These methods will be used to map vector hotspots and quantify infection rates across agricultural (cocoa farms) and residential (peri-urban) sites. Unlike prior studies relying primarily on morphological identification, the molecular approach adapted will resolve cryptic species complexes like An. gambiae s.l. This directly address the National Malaria Elimination Programme’s (2023) call for precision surveillance. The findings from this work will inform targeted interventions, like management of site-specific larval source in farmlands and the distribution of bed net in endemic areas of the community with high-biting-rate. By linking geospatial data with entomological inoculation rates (EIR), this work will provide a replicable framework for controlling malaria in rapidly changing landscapes. This study represents one of the first molecular surveillance (PCR) efforts targeting Anopheles vectors in Western North Ghana, a region where agricultural expansion and urbanization are driving spatially variable malaria transmission patterns. Mapping species-specific Plasmodium infection rates to land-use types will provide actionable insights for NMEP on addressing the gaps in current morphological surveillance.' i want more current and relevant references
